blocks.p: Groups reflect model profiles, not tournament rankings.
These are fixed starting cohorts, not current ladder ranks or mutually exclusive universal model types.

Each setup stays in the group it started in, the original league it played in before any league move, with that group's own match points: only matches between setups of the same starting group count, wherever they were played (league season, ladder round or gap match); late entries are left out. 3 points a win, 1 a draw. Ties: points, then head-to-head (a mini-table of the matches among three or more), then the lower error rate (rule set on 28 Oct, after the ties were known; no place here needed the error rate). GNUbg weak, the anchor program, is in all three groups. A setup that moved between leagues keeps its row here; where it plays now is in After league moves.

Badges: Hype Cup seed a Cup place (Cups) · ↑ now in League N ↓ now in League N ↕ back in League N league moves, from the ladder's records. Match points are match results only; they are not the Risk, Quality or Confidence measures.

blocks.p: Error rate and risk judgement: 95% intervals, whole games resampled. Ability d′ and caution c at the 0.001 margin: rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; 95% intervals, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Cut off: answers that stopped at an output limit the request sent (finish reason length, stop reason max_tokens, finishReason MAX_TOKENS, incomplete max_output_tokens), in the stored response or error. Effort: the reasoning effort the requests sent. Engine's best play: the share of its scored decisions that chose the engine's best play (equity loss under the best-play threshold). Time: median request seconds per decision (waits between retries not included). Cost per 1,000 decisions: the recorded tokens at the price shown, as labelled there (list or billed price; for a setup on our GPUs the hosted model's list price, not billed). Every match of every stage: Matches.

blocks.p: Risk calls per setup: was each risk the right one, and was safe right when it played safe? 100 = every call right, 50 = always safe; the line on each bar is its 95% interval (games resampled) · higher is better

blocks.p: Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.
Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.
Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

blocks.p: Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.
Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.
Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

blocks.p: Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.
Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.
Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

blocks.p: Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.
Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.
Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

blocks.p: Every model with both settings in this league's games is listed. Risk judgement (margin 0.001, 95% intervals from resampling whole games) and error rate are two separate measures: the "Error rate, in league play" column is about error rate only and says nothing about risk judgement. The risk judgement change is the higher setting minus the lower, from unrounded values. Whether two intervals overlap describes them; it is not a test of a difference.

League games are not the same positions, so this comparison is not paired and shows no effect of the setting: a higher or lower value at the higher setting is not evidence that reasoning caused it. For error rate it reads "lower/higher error rate in league play" only when the two 95% intervals do not overlap, and "no clear difference in league play" otherwise. The paired verdict waits for the shared positions.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B: it has no effort setting. (off): an empty thinking block is prefilled, so it answers without thinking. (on): it is let to think before it answers (its template has no switch or effort setting; the "low" its requests carry is ignored).

groups.title: Can a model predict where it will waver?

blocks.p: Stage B: five teams
Close choices: does a setup know where it hesitates?

Scope. Gemma 4 31B on · NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell + NVIDIA DGX Spark was started but not completed: two reboots and a GPU fault interrupted it, and it was stopped after 311 of 500 play calls on 2026-10-25. Its partial data is not reported.

Each team answered the same 100 positions 5 times, and once more in a separate call naming the features it expects to differ between the plays it might choose (hitting risk, making a point, the race, the prime). Observed set: the features that differ between any of the 5 chosen plays. Primary score: exact agreement of the predicted set with the observed set. Secondary score, declared secondary: partial overlap of the two sets. Baseline: the team's own predictions shuffled within phase, 1,000 seeded shuffles; p = the share of shuffles scoring at least the observed mean. Stage B asks again and looks at repeated answers; it is separate from stage A (Confidence tab), which reads recorded league decisions.

blocks.p: Earlier version: plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early. When Gemini 4 Argon answered the same 1,000 positions with the plays shuffled, its error rate changed by +1.9 (95% interval −0.2 to +4.2), so the effect is not proven.

Earlier version The sections below are kept from the earlier report, unchanged. Their numbers come from the earlier version and are never ranked with current numbers. The prompt and how it was built are on the Method page.
Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.

Each model plays every other model once per league (a single round robin). A match is played in rounds of two games with the same dice: in the second game the players swap seats and the same sequence of rolls is repeated, so both face the same luck. Games score 1 point, 2 for a gammon and 3 for a backgammon; there is no doubling cube.

blocks.li: Match length: 3 rounds, or fewer: the first player to 5 points after a full round (both games) wins if ahead. A tie gets one extra round, then counts as a draw.
League table: 3 points for a match win, 1 for a draw; ties broken by more games won, then fewer games lost.
Turn limit: a game still running after 300 turns (both sides counted) goes to the lower pip count for 1 point.
Clock: 30 seconds free per decision, then a 5-minute bank per game. Running out loses the game.
Legality: the program generates every legal play and the model chooses one of them, so a model can never make an illegal move. A roll with only one legal play is played automatically.
Memory: every decision is a separate request. Models are not told how earlier games went.

blocks.p: With seven models, each league has 21 matches and one model sits out each matchday. A match starts as soon as both of its models are free, and no model plays two matches at once.
Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.
All seven answer the same kind of request: a text state and one choice question whose options are the legal plays. Two are hosted services; the other five run on our own GPUs.
TypeSafe's decision model, served through its System One API; the request format the others copy.

blocks.h: GPT-6 Luna · OpenAI Decisions API, hosted

blocks.p: OpenAI's decision endpoint with gpt-6-luna. The only one that sometimes declines to choose; that happened 3 times in early leagues, on positions with 97 to 439 legal plays, and never in the current format.

blocks.h: Perplexity Decider 27B v1.1 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell + NVIDIA DGX Spark · Perplexity, self-hosted

blocks.p: The released pplx-decider-v1.1-27b checkpoint, run with its own server code. It accepts up to 8,192 tokens, so long play lists are sent in groups of 25 (see below). It replaced Perplexity's hosted Decider 27B from league #6 on.
A 27B decision model that scores all options in one pass. Groups of up to 110 options.

blocks.h: Open-Jev-27B-v1.1 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell · open reimplementation of Jev, self-hosted

blocks.p: A LoRA adapter and decision head on a 27B base model. It scores every option as its own sequence that repeats the whole question, with a 4,096-token limit per sequence, which is what limits the prompt's length for every model.
Google's gemma-4-12B-it, unchanged, behind a server that labels the options A, B, C… and reads the model's probability for each letter. Groups of up to 26 options.

blocks.h: Gemma 4 31B · our configuration of the Cygnet recipe

blocks.p: The same letter-reading server in front of gemma-4-31B-it, served in FP8. Not a trained decision model: a general chat model whose answer-letter probabilities are read directly. Its calibration setting was fitted for Cygnet's 12B model; that changes its reported confidence, not which play it picks.

When a position has more legal plays than a model's group size, the plays are split into equal groups, the model picks a winner in each, then chooses among the winners. Liquid's d1 played in the early leagues and was dropped after its free tier rate-limited a league to a stop.
Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.

Wins and losses depend heavily on the dice. A backgammon engine can instead judge every decision directly: for each move it finds the best play, and measures how much winning chance, in equity (expected points per game), the chosen play gave away. Averaged over all decisions and multiplied by 500, this is the error rate (performance rating, PR) that backgammon players use, here for checker plays only; forced moves are not counted. eXtreme Gammon's human scale: under 2.5 world champion, 2.5 to 5 world class, 5 to 7.5 expert, 7.5 to 12.5 advanced, 12.5 to 17.5 intermediate, 17.5 to 22.5 casual, 22.5 to 30 beginner, 30 or more distracted. Human ratings also count doubling cube decisions, which these games do not have, so the comparison is approximate.

We scored all 104,045 decisions the models made in every league with GNU Backgammon 1.08. Every legal play was evaluated at 0-ply, then the five best and the chosen play again at 2-ply; the loss is the 2-ply equity of the best play minus that of the chosen one. As a check, on the opening roll the plays that the rollout table calls best lose 0.0002 equity on average, other plays 0.063.

blocks.p: Error rate: mean equity lost per decision × 500, with a 95% interval that treats decisions as independent (moves within a game are not, so the true interval is somewhat wider). "Engine's best play": share of decisions where the chosen play lost less than 0.001. "Blunders": decisions losing more than 0.08 equity. The last four columns are the error rate in each league; #13 adds the move history.

blocks.li: The engine ranks the models almost as the league tables do. Gemma 4 31B is clearly best and Open-Jev 27B clearly worst. Decider v1.1, Jev, Clef and GPT-6 Luna are within about one interval of each other, which is why their league places move around; Cygnet is a little behind them.
Every model blunders often: from one move in five (Gemma 4 31B) to one in three (Open-Jev 27B). Even Gemma 4 31B chooses the engine's best play only about half the time.
The prompt mattered more than the model. Before move consequences were computed, the whole field averaged 120 to 138; after, 36 to 40. The worst model now is better than the average model was then.

blocks.p: "Safest play": the option whose position the opponent hits with the fewest of its 36 rolls, read from the numbers the model was shown. "Shots left": opponent rolls out of 36 that hit after the chosen play. Both are measured on decisions sent as a single request (about 1,700 to 2,100 per model); the safest available play left 2.7 to 4.2 shots on average, a typical option about 13.

blocks.li: Gemma 4 31B is the strongest player here, and it is not a trained decision model: a general chat model whose answer-letter probabilities are read. It lost 3 of 18 matches and won the most gammons.

Safe is not the same as good. GPT-6 Luna picks the safest play most often and leaves the fewest shots, yet finished 5th in all three leagues. Winning also takes making points and building a prime, which costs some risk; Gemma and Clef take more risk and win more gammons.

Open-Jev 27B collapsed in this format. It finished 2nd in league #3, where options were just notations, and last in every league since, with the most shots left and the highest error rate. We have not found out why; the numbers it is shown are the same as everyone else's.
Speed does not decide it. The three fastest models are spread across the table, and no model came close to its clock.

groups.title: Can a team beat the best model?

blocks.p: Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.

Every model reports a probability for each option. If those probabilities say when a model is right, a team could ask all seven and play the answer of whichever is most sure. To test this, we sent the same 1,000 recorded positions (2 to 25 legal plays each, drawn from leagues #8, #11, #12 and #13) to all seven models with exactly the request the original player received, and scored every legal play with GNU Backgammon at 2-ply: 7,000 answers and 9,439 evaluated plays. Any team and any rule can then be scored offline on the same positions.

blocks.h: Confidence says how hard a position is, not who is right

blocks.p: Within each model, confidence does carry information: across its league decisions, a model is right more often when it is more confident (AUROC 0.66 to 0.74, where 0.5 is chance). But the models use very different scales:

head: Model
Engine's best play
Average stated probability
When it is most sure
it is right
rows: Perplexity Decider 27B v1.1 · NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell + NVIDIA DGX Spark

blocks.p: From 17,579 league decisions sent as a single request; "right" means the engine's best play (loss below 0.001 equity). The stated probability is the one the model gave its chosen play; the models' own "confidence" fields are defined differently from one another, so they are not used.

Clef and Open-Jev look like the most reliable models when they are sure, but they are only sure on easy positions, where everyone else is right as well. The test that matters is what happens when models disagree on the same position:

head: When Gemma 4 31B and this model disagree
Gemma has the better play
The more confident model has the better play
rows: Perplexity Decider 27B v1.1 · NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell + NVIDIA DGX Spark

blocks.p: Following the more confident model is never better than simply following Gemma 4 31B.

head: Team and rule
Error rate
Engine's best play
Difference from Gemma alone (95%)
rows: Best of 120 formations: Clef + Decider v1.1 + Gemma, probabilities added up
Oracle: the best answer any of the 7 gave

blocks.p: Error rate on the 1,000 shared positions (lower is better). Calibrated rules map each model's stated probability to its observed accuracy or loss with isotonic regression, fitted on one half of the positions and scored on the other (two-fold cross-fitting). Intervals are bootstrap intervals over positions, paired with Gemma 4 31B on the same positions. The best formation was chosen on the same positions it is scored on, which flatters it.

blocks.li: No team beats the best single model. Raw confidence ties with Gemma 4 31B only because its inflated probabilities win almost every vote; correcting the scales makes the team worse.

The room for a team is large. Gemma 4 31B misses the engine's best play on 456 of the 1,000 positions, and on a third of those another model found it. An oracle would halve the error rate. What is missing is a way to tell which answer is the right one.
The data is kept for further formations. Other selectors (agreement between models, the number of legal plays, the stage of the game) can be tested on the same 1,000 positions without new requests.

blocks.p: Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.

Measured on the same 1,000 recorded positions as the team test, with exactly the request each original player received. Besides the seven league players, the table includes general language models we tried the same way: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash Next and GLM-4.7-Flash are read through their probabilities for each answer letter, like Gemma 4 31B. GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 3.8 Flash return no such probabilities: each answers one letter, constrained to the option letters, at low reasoning effort (Gemini's lowest available level). Gemini 4 Argon reported no reasoning tokens at that level, so it answered directly. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash also ran a second time with reasoning on (lowest effort), answering one constrained letter after reasoning. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 ran through ChatGPT and Claude subscriptions.

blocks.p: Error rate on the 1,000 shared positions (lower is better). Time is wall-clock per request, from sending it to receiving the answer, with the stated number of requests in flight. Our GPUs are NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards with 96 GB each, in one machine. The seven league players were asked together, so the self-hosted ones shared the machine; the other models were each asked alone. A run of GLM-5.3-Flash is left out: it played close to random, most likely because of how we had to run it on this machine.

The plays are listed in the order the runner generated them, which tends to put the best play early. Asked again with the same plays in a random order, Gemini 4 Argon's error rate rose from 16.9 to 18.9 (difference 1.9, 95% interval −0.3 to 4.1): probably a small help from the order, not yet a proven one. The next version of the benchmark shuffles the plays for every model.

Cost basis: the provider's list price × the tokens its API reported; the bill itself was not checked. Jev 1.13 ($0.042 per 1M input tokens, output free) and GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI's Decisions API ($0.10 per 1M input tokens, output free): prices of 8 October 2026, tokens averaged over their league decisions with 2 to 25 legal plays (3,740 and 3,238 input tokens per decision). Gemini 3.8 Flash ($0.75 per 1M input tokens, $3.75 per 1M output tokens, reasoning billed as output; introductory price of 8 October 2026, which doubles on 1 January 2027): tokens measured on 100 of the positions, 3,373 input and 192 output per decision on average. Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per 1M input, $10 per 1M output; price until 30 November 2026, doubling on 1 December): tokens reported for all 1,000 positions, 3,462 input and 5 output per decision. GPT-6 Astra ($10 per 1M input, $50 per 1M output) and Claude Opus 5.5 ($4 input, $20 output): API list prices of 8 October 2026 × the tokens reported for all 1,000 positions (3,213 input and 86 output, and 4,424 input and 198 output per decision). Both ran on subscriptions, which are not billed per token, so these are API-equivalent estimates. Self-hosted models have no per-request price; a 7-model league of about 690 decisions per player took about 30 minutes on the four GPUs. DeepSeek with reasoning used 6,657 output tokens per decision on average.

blocks.li: The cheapest strong player is one we run ourselves. Gemma 4 31B costs only GPU time, needs one card, and answers in about 0.6 s.

The best players cost most and are slowest. GPT-6 Astra makes the fewest errors by far, but at API prices it costs about a hundred times as much per decision as GPT-6 Luna, and one decision in ten takes 11 seconds or more. Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5 show no clear difference (16.9 against 17.3; difference 0.3, 95% interval −1.9 to 2.5), with Argon about a third of Opus's price; Gemini 3.8 Flash (18.3) is close behind at half Argon's price. Even asking Astra, Opus and Gemini 3.8 Flash together and taking the majority answer is worse than Astra alone (14.4).

Reasoning helps an open model a lot, at a steep time cost. With reasoning on, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's error rate falls from 27.5 to 18.1 (95% interval of the gain 6.1 to 12.7), close to Opus's, but a decision takes about 100 seconds instead of half a second.
The hosted decision services are fastest and cheapest per decision, at about 0.2 s and well under a dollar per 1,000 decisions, but they play worse than Gemma 4 31B.

blocks.p: Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.

blocks.li: Small sample. Three finished leagues of 21 matches in the main format, about 340 games. Placings in the middle of the table move from league to league; the error rate is the steadier measure.

The engine evaluation is not the strongest available. Moves are judged at 2-ply with GNU Backgammon, not by full rollouts or eXtreme Gammon, and in cubeless money equity: the games have no doubling cube, and match score is ignored. Small differences between close plays can be wrong, but the losses that count as blunders and the gaps between models are much larger than that.

Models only play each other. Their absolute strength against human or engine players is unknown. On the engine's scale none of them reaches expert level; the best, GPT-6 Astra, plays like an advanced human.
Configuration matters. Five models run on servers set up by us, and Gemma 4 31B uses a recipe built for a different model. Hosted services can change without notice.

The prompt steers. The question and the strategy text say what a good move looks like, so the results measure how well models follow that guidance with the numbers in front of them, as much as how well they play.
